sections.title: Node 0 — A language that cannot do anything
sections.content:
What this node is trying to establish: before we reason about the browser, the DOM, window, document, fetch, timers, the event loop, or rendering, we need to separate three ideas that frontend tutorials constantly blur together: the JavaScript language, the JavaScript engine, and the host environment.

The original landscape makes a deliberately provocative claim: JavaScript, considered only as a language, cannot do anything outside computation. That wording sounds absurd at first because you have personally written console.log(), fetch(), setTimeout(), document.querySelector(), and localStorage.getItem(). The point is not that those calls are fake. The point is that they come from different layers.

1. Start with the thing you actually write: ECMAScript

When you write:

const price = 100;
const tax = 18;
const total = price + tax;

the JavaScript language gives you rules for all of this. It tells the engine what const means, how a variable is bound, what a number is, what + means for two numbers, how expressions are evaluated, and what value results from the computation.

That is already a lot. The language gives you primitive values, objects, arrays, functions, lexical scope, closures, prototypes, classes, operators, control flow, exceptions, promises, modules, and a large collection of standard built-ins such as Math, JSON, Map, Set, RegExp, Intl, and Date.

But notice what is missing. There is no language construct that says:

show this value on the user's monitor
read bytes from /etc/passwd
open a TCP connection
ask the operating system for the current pixel buffer
turn on the user's microphone
create a browser tab

The ECMAScript specification primarily defines computation and language semantics. It deliberately does not define a universal filesystem, window system, network stack, camera API, terminal, browser, or operating system interface.

2. Why this is not as weird as it sounds

JavaScript was designed to be embedded in different products. A language that permanently assumed it was running in a web browser would have been a very poor general-purpose embedded language.

Instead, the design is roughly:

language specification
        +
implementation of that language
        +
host-provided capabilities
        =
a usable JavaScript environment

The same JavaScript syntax can therefore exist inside radically different hosts.

EnvironmentTypical host capabilities
BrowserDOM, events, network APIs, storage, graphics, timers, browser security model
Node.jsFilesystem, processes, sockets, streams, OS integration, timers
DenoWeb-platform-style APIs plus explicit permissions for OS access
Worker-style web hostNetworking, messaging and timers, but no normal page DOM

So the statement “JavaScript can read files” is incomplete. A more precise statement is: “JavaScript running inside a host that exposes filesystem APIs can read files through those host APIs.”

3. The JavaScript engine is not the browser

This is the next distinction that removes a lot of mystery.

                 Your source code
                        │
                        ▼
                JavaScript engine
                        │
                        ▼
                  Host environment

An engine such as V8, SpiderMonkey, or JavaScriptCore implements the JavaScript language. It parses JavaScript, creates the internal structures needed to execute it, performs the computations defined by the language, and manages the engine's own execution machinery.

But V8 is not “Chrome”. V8 does not inherently mean “there is a DOM”, “there is a URL bar”, or “there is a document object”. Another host can embed the same engine and expose completely different APIs.

A useful analogy is:

ECMAScript = the rules of a language
V8        = an implementation that can execute that language
Browser   = a host that embeds an engine and supplies browser capabilities

4. So where did console, fetch, and setTimeout come from?

This is the practical test of whether you actually understand the separation.

console.log("hello");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("later");
}, 1000);

fetch("/api/users");

document.querySelector("#app");

None of these names was introduced by your local source file. More importantly, they do not all belong to the same specification or implementation layer.

The browser host exposes a JavaScript-visible environment containing objects and functions that ultimately connect your program to browser-managed machinery.

Conceptually:

browser host
   │
   ├── exposes console
   ├── exposes timers
   ├── exposes fetch
   ├── exposes DOM-related objects
   ├── exposes storage APIs
   └── exposes many more Web APIs
            │
            ▼
      JavaScript code can call them

This does not mean that the browser literally builds one gigantic object using the exact source syntax const window = { ... }. It is a mental model for understanding the JavaScript-visible surface of a much larger native/browser implementation.

5. The object insight that makes browser APIs stop looking magical

Your recent understanding of JavaScript objects is exactly the right foundation here.

At the language level, an object can be understood as a collection of properties. For example:

const user = {
  name: "Devansh",
  age: 21
};

Then:

user.name
user.age

means property access. The expression on the left produces an object, and the property name on the right selects a property from it.

That same basic idea is extremely useful when looking at browser APIs. When you see:

document.title
document.querySelector("#app")
window.location
navigator.userAgent

you can stop treating the words document, window, and navigator as mysterious pieces of special syntax. They are JavaScript-visible values. Those values have properties and methods. Those properties and methods connect the JavaScript program to browser-managed capabilities.

For example, a method is not a completely separate category from a property. A method is a function-valued property used as an operation associated with an object.

const calculator = {
  add: (a, b) => a + b
};

calculator.add(2, 3);

The property is add. Its value happens to be a function. Calling that function through the object is commonly described as calling the object's method.

So when you read:

document.querySelector("#app")

the useful first-principles interpretation is:

document       → obtain a JavaScript-visible object
.querySelector → access a function-valued property/method
(...)          → call it

What makes the method powerful is not some magical new kind of JavaScript syntax. The function is implemented by the browser/platform and is connected to browser-managed state.

6. A browser API does not mean “the browser changed the JavaScript language”

This is another common mental trap.

Seeing:

fetch(...)
window(...)
document(...)
setTimeout(...)

can make it feel as though the language itself somehow contains every browser feature. It does not.

The browser creates a runtime environment in which JavaScript has access to additional objects, functions, constructors and host hooks. The source code is still ordinary JavaScript code accessing values supplied by the environment.

That distinction is also why this works:

typeof document

in a browser but fails or produces a different result in a non-browser host. The JavaScript syntax did not change. The environment changed.

7. What is a “runtime,” then?

The word runtime is used loosely in engineering. In the sense relevant to this topic, it means the machinery and host-provided environment that exists while your program is running and through which your code can interact with the outside world.

A browser runtime is therefore not best imagined as one little executable box called “the runtime”. It is an architectural collection of components.

                 BROWSER HOST / RUNTIME
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
        │                                      │
        │  JavaScript engine                   │
        │                                      │
        │  Host/Web APIs                       │
        │    • DOM                             │
        │    • events                          │
        │    • fetch/network integration       │
        │    • timers                          │
        │    • storage                         │
        │    • media                           │
        │                                      │
        │  Scheduling / event-loop machinery   │
        │                                      │
        │  Rendering machinery                 │
        │                                      │
        │  Security / origin enforcement       │
        │                                      │
        └──────────────────────────────────────┘

Later nodes will take these boxes apart. For now, the important point is simply that “browser runtime” is a useful architectural label for the environment surrounding the language implementation.

8. The global object: why does window seem to be everywhere?

Every JavaScript execution environment has a global environment. JavaScript code needs some mechanism through which globally available bindings and host-provided facilities become reachable.

In a normal browser page, the global object is exposed through window.

window
 ├── document
 ├── location
 ├── navigator
 ├── console
 ├── localStorage
 ├── setTimeout
 ├── fetch
 └── ...

Again, treat this as a conceptual picture rather than an exact source-level object literal. Some things are global bindings, some are properties, and the browser platform has a much richer Web IDL/native implementation beneath them.

globalThis is the standardized language-level way to refer to the global object without pretending that every JavaScript host calls it window. In a page, globalThis is the browser global object; other environments expose their own global object through the same portable name.

9. Why you can write document without writing window.document

This is one of those things that feels magical until you separate lexical bindings from object-property access.

In a traditional browser page, many global names are made available through the global environment. That is why code can commonly write:

document.querySelector("#app");

rather than:

window.document.querySelector("#app");

The two forms are related, but do not mentally collapse all global bindings into “everything is literally a property lookup on window.” The global environment has its own semantics, and the browser integrates host-defined globals into it.

10. Then what exactly is document?

This is where your earlier DOM confusion starts becoming tractable.

document is a JavaScript-visible object representing the current document in the browser's DOM environment. It is not the original HTML file. It is not merely a string containing the HTML. And it is not a magical keyword built into ECMAScript.

The browser receives a document resource, parses HTML, and constructs an in-memory representation. The JavaScript-visible document value gives your program access to that representation through DOM APIs.

So conceptually:

HTML bytes/text arrive
        │
        ▼
HTML parser
        │
        ▼
DOM / document structure in browser-managed memory
        │
        ▼
document object exposed to JavaScript

Later, Node 1 will turn this into a full explanation of how the browser goes from a URL to HTML bytes to a parsed document tree and eventually a running program. We are deliberately stopping just before that machinery because Node 1 exists to answer the remaining question.

11. Why “Document Object Model” has three words

The name is easier to understand when you separate the words instead of treating DOM as one incantation.

Document means the structured resource being represented: the page/document the browser is currently working with.

Object means that the programming interface exposes parts of this world as programmatically manipulable objects with properties, methods, identity and relationships.

Model means the program is not handed the original textual representation as its primary interface. It is handed a structured representation — a model of the document that can be queried and mutated.

So “Document Object Model” is essentially saying: a program-facing object model representing a document.

This is not a claim that the DOM is a simple JavaScript object literal. Browser DOM objects are backed by browser implementation machinery, and their interfaces are standardized through the web platform. The useful mental model is that JavaScript sees a graph/tree of objects that represents document state.

12. Your memory model intuition is useful, with one important correction

You described JavaScript objects as data stored in memory and imagined them as nodes connected in a graph. That is a very useful intuition for learning object identity and references.

For example:

const address = { city: "Delhi" };
const user = { name: "Devansh", address };

Conceptually you can picture:

user object
   │
   └── address ─────► address object
                         │
                         └── city → "Delhi"

That helps explain why changing address.city is observable through user.address.city: both references lead to the same underlying object.

But do not take the phrase “object = contiguous memory block with a fixed shape” too literally. JavaScript implementations are free to use sophisticated internal layouts, hidden classes/shapes, inline caches, pointer compression and other optimization techniques. The language-level truth is about objects, properties, identity and references, not about one mandated physical memory representation.

The DOM graph is similarly a language-facing model, not a promise that every DOM node is implemented as one plain JavaScript object allocated in the same way as an ordinary object literal.

13. Why document.querySelector() is a perfect bridge between the language and the host

Consider:

const button = document.querySelector("#save");

There are several layers hiding inside this one line:

document
   ↓
JavaScript-visible host object
   ↓
.querySelector
   ↓
method/property lookup
   ↓
call with a string argument
   ↓
browser DOM implementation searches its document model
   ↓
returns a JavaScript-visible object or null

The syntax of property lookup and function calls is ordinary JavaScript. The special power comes from the fact that the value and method are connected to the browser's DOM implementation.

14. Why this matters for debugging

Once you have this separation, debugging becomes much more systematic.

If something like:

const x = 2 + 3;

behaves incorrectly, you are probably dealing with a language/engine problem or a misunderstanding of JavaScript semantics.

If:

document.querySelector("#app")

returns null, the issue may be about the document state, parsing order, selector matching, or when the code ran.

If:

fetch("/api/users")

fails, the problem may involve URL resolution, networking, origin policy, HTTP, service workers, caching, credentials, or a server — none of which is “the JavaScript language” in the narrow sense.

If:

setTimeout(fn, 1000)

does not behave how you expect, you are entering host scheduling semantics and eventually the event loop.

The same syntax can therefore take you into completely different layers of the stack.

15. The most useful classification habit

When you encounter something in JavaScript code, ask:

“Who owns this concept or API?”
ThingUseful first classification
constJavaScript language
Object / Array / FunctionJavaScript language
PromiseJavaScript language abstraction
MathJavaScript built-in
documentBrowser / Web platform
windowBrowser global environment
fetchWeb platform API
setTimeoutHost/Web-platform scheduling API
localStorageWeb platform storage API
fs.readFile()Node.js host API

This one habit prevents a huge amount of conceptual mixing.

16. A question you might immediately have: “Then why does JavaScript even have asynchronous things like Promise?”

Because “asynchronous” and “external I/O” are not exactly the same concept.

The JavaScript language defines the Promise abstraction and the semantics of promise reactions. The host environment can perform external work and later cause JavaScript-visible promise machinery to progress.

A promise is therefore not itself the browser's network card, timer or event loop. It is a language-level abstraction for representing an eventual result and composing reactions around that result.

This distinction becomes crucial later when we explain how promises, microtasks and the event loop fit together. For Node 0, keep the boundary clear: the language can define an abstraction for an eventual value without itself owning every external mechanism that produces that value.

17. Another question: “So is the browser runtime just a giant JavaScript object?”

No. A JavaScript program needs a JavaScript-visible interface, but the actual implementation is much larger.

Underneath an API such as the DOM there can be browser-native objects, C++/Rust implementation code depending on the engine/browser component, internal browser state, networking code, security checks, rendering state, OS integration, IPC between processes, and scheduling infrastructure.

From JavaScript, however, you interact with a standardized object interface. That is why your object intuition is valuable even though it is not a literal description of every byte in memory.

18. The complete mental model for Node 0

                    YOUR JAVASCRIPT CODE
                              │
                              ▼
                      JavaScript language
                    (syntax + semantics)
                              │
                              ▼
                       JS engine
                 (executes the language)
                              │
                              ▼
                      HOST / RUNTIME
          ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
          │                   │                   │
       Web APIs           Scheduling          Other host
          │                   │                machinery
          │                   │                   │
        DOM                timers              storage
        fetch             event loop           media
        events             tasks               network
          │                   │                   │
          └───────────────────┴───────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    operating system / hardware

The browser is therefore not “JavaScript.” The browser is a host environment that embeds a JavaScript engine and supplies a large collection of additional capabilities and surrounding machinery.

19. What you should now be able to explain without hand-waving

Question: Is fetch a JavaScript language feature?

Answer: No. It is a Web platform API exposed to JavaScript by the browser environment.

Question: Is V8 the browser?

Answer: No. V8 is a JavaScript engine. A browser can embed an engine and surround it with many other components.

Question: Is document a JavaScript keyword?

Answer: No. It is a browser-provided JavaScript-visible global associated with the DOM/document environment.

Question: Is a method a completely different thing from a property?

Answer: No. A method is commonly a function-valued property that is used as an operation associated with an object.

Question: Is the DOM the HTML source text?

Answer: No. The HTML is an input representation. The DOM is a browser-maintained structured model exposed through objects and APIs.

Question: Why can browser JavaScript use window, but Node.js code normally does not?

Answer: Because they are different host environments with different global environments and capabilities.

20. The boundary this node intentionally leaves unresolved

We have now established who provides the capabilities, but not yet how the browser gets your program into existence in the first place.

We have said:

person enters URL
        ↓
browser gets a document
        ↓
browser exposes a runtime
        ↓
JavaScript runs

but we have not explained the machinery between those arrows.

Where did the HTML bytes come from? Who parses them? When does the DOM appear? What exactly happens when the parser encounters a <script> tag? Why does a script in the middle of HTML block parsing? What do defer, async, and modules change? When does document become safe to use? When does the top-level JavaScript actually execute?

Those are precisely the questions Node 1 exists to answer.

Node 0's takeaway: stop saying “the browser gives JavaScript magical powers.” Say instead: JavaScript is a language executed by an engine inside a host environment, and that host exposes additional capabilities through JavaScript-visible APIs. Once that separation becomes automatic, document, window, fetch, setTimeout, and eventually the entire browser runtime stop looking like unrelated magic and start looking like different pieces of one architecture.

sections.title: Node 1 — How a page becomes a running program
sections.content:
What this node is trying to explain: Node 0 separated the JavaScript language from the host environment and left one precise question: if JavaScript is only a language and the browser is the host, where does the running JavaScript program come from in the first place? This node traces the chain from a URL, to bytes, to HTML text, to parsing, to the DOM, to a script being executed, to a JavaScript environment that already contains browser-provided objects.

The single most useful mental model for this node is:

URL
  ↓
resource request
  ↓
bytes arrive
  ↓
HTML parser
  ↓
DOM / document structure
  ↓
<script> encountered
  ↓
JavaScript source is obtained
  ↓
JavaScript engine executes it
  ↓
your code runs inside a browser-provided environment

Every arrow matters. Most frontend confusion comes from jumping over several of them and saying “the browser runs the page” as though that were one operation.

1. Start with the question Node 0 left behind

Node 0 established that ECMAScript itself does not define the browser. It gives you the language rules, but the browser host gives your running program capabilities such as the DOM, networking APIs, timers and browser-specific global bindings.

But none of that answers the first practical question:

How does the browser get from “the user opened this URL” to “this JavaScript program is currently executing”?

That is what Node 1 traces.

Imagine clicking:

https://example.com/app.html

There is no JavaScript program floating in the URL. The browser has to obtain a resource, interpret the response, discover what resources it references, construct an in-memory representation of the document, and eventually execute any JavaScript it encounters.

So when you say “the browser loaded the page,” that phrase hides a sequence of different operations.

2. A URL is an instruction for finding a resource, not the page itself

A URL is a structured identifier. It gives the browser enough information to determine which resource you are referring to and where to request it from.

https://example.com/app.html
└──┬──┘ └───────┬───────┘
   │            │
 scheme        host + path

The browser uses the URL to determine how to obtain the resource. With a normal HTTPS URL, that involves the network stack, DNS, a connection to the server, HTTP, and eventually a response body containing bytes.

Do not mentally equate:

URL = HTML

Instead think:

URL
 ↓
identifier for a resource
 ↓
request
 ↓
response
 ↓
bytes

Those bytes might represent HTML, JavaScript, CSS, an image, JSON, or something else depending on the resource.

3. The browser initially receives bytes, not a DOM

This is one of the most important transitions in the whole topic.

The network does not deliver:

Node
  children
    properties
      methods

as a ready-made JavaScript object tree.

It delivers bytes. For an HTML resource, those bytes are decoded into text according to the document's encoding rules, and the HTML parser consumes that text.

network
  ↓
bytes
  ↓
decoded HTML text
  ↓
HTML parser

So when you open page source in a browser, you are looking at something conceptually much closer to the textual source representation that was delivered than to the live object model used by JavaScript.

4. HTML is text; the DOM is a separate live representation

This is the distinction that should finally break the old “DOM = HTML” mental block.

Suppose the response contains:

<div id="app">
  <button>Save</button>
</div>

That is text. It is a sequence of characters which obey HTML parsing rules.

The browser then parses that text and builds a structured document representation.

Conceptually:

HTML text

"<div id='app'> ..."

        ↓ parser

DOM tree

Document
  │
  └── html
       │
       └── body
            │
            └── div
                 └── button

The DOM is therefore not “the HTML string with methods attached.” It is a browser-managed object model created from the HTML source.

This is why the two can diverge.

JavaScript can do:

document.querySelector("#app").textContent = "Saved";

The live DOM changes. The browser can render the new state. But the original HTML resource sitting on the server has not been edited.

5. “Then what exactly is the document?”

This is where the three words in Document Object Model become useful rather than ceremonial.

Document is the document the browser is currently representing: the page/document resource and its parsed state.

Object means the programming interface exposes pieces of that state through JavaScript-visible objects with identity, properties, methods and relationships.

Model means the browser gives your program a structured representation of the document rather than requiring you to manipulate the original HTML text as the primary interface.

So:

The DOM is a program-facing object model of a document.

That sentence is much more useful than memorising “DOM stands for Document Object Model.”

6. Your recent JavaScript-object insight fits perfectly here

You recently reduced a JavaScript object to a much simpler idea: a value with properties, where a property has a key and a value, and a function-valued property is commonly called a method.

That mental model is exactly the right starting point for understanding why browser APIs stop looking magical.

For your own object:

const user = {
  name: "Devansh",
  age: 21
};

the expression:

user.name

means: obtain the object referred to by user, then access its name property.

For a DOM object, the same language-level idea of property access still exists:

document.title
document.body
document.querySelector

What changes is what the object represents and how the implementation behind that object works.

A DOM object is not merely a normal object literal you could reproduce with:

const document = {
  title: "...",
  body: ...,
  querySelector: ...
};

That would be a useful toy model, but it would not be the browser implementation.

The real browser maintains document state and native/browser machinery, and exposes standardized interfaces into that state.

7. DOM nodes are JavaScript-visible objects, but they are not “just ordinary object literals”

This distinction is worth making very carefully because it will keep coming back.

When JavaScript does:

const button = document.querySelector("button");

the value stored in button is a JavaScript-visible object representing a DOM element.

You can then perform ordinary JavaScript operations against it:

button.textContent
button.id
button.className
button.addEventListener(...)

From JavaScript's point of view, that is a perfectly legitimate object with properties and methods.

But underneath that interface, the browser is maintaining much richer state than a plain object literal would suggest: node relationships, document ownership, event targets, rendering information, styles, layout state and other browser-managed data.

So your mental model can be:

JavaScript-visible DOM object
        │
        ▼
browser-managed document state

That model is both intuitive and accurate enough for the level of reasoning we need here.

8. The DOM is a tree, but the browser has more than one graph

The DOM is called a tree because parent/child relationships in the document form a tree-shaped structure.

Document
  └── html
       ├── head
       │    └── ...
       └── body
            ├── header
            └── main
                 └── button

But your broader “objects connected in memory” intuition is still useful.

There are references from one JavaScript-visible object to another. A DOM element has a parent, children, attributes and relationships to other browser concepts. The browser itself has many more internal structures that are not simply the DOM tree.

So do not collapse these statements:

DOM = tree
DOM = all browser state
DOM = all JavaScript objects
DOM = one contiguous memory block

None of those stronger statements is correct.

The useful statement is:

The DOM is a tree-shaped object model of the document, exposed through browser APIs and backed by browser-managed state.

9. Parsing happens incrementally, not as one giant “build DOM” button

The browser does not necessarily wait until every byte of the HTML has arrived before doing anything.

The HTML parser can consume the incoming document incrementally.

bytes arrive
   ↓
decode
   ↓
parse some HTML
   ↓
construct more DOM
   ↓
discover more resources
   ↓
continue parsing

This explains why a page can begin loading before the entire document has arrived.

It also explains why the location of a script element can matter: parsing and script execution interact.

10. The parser reaches a classic <script> and something important happens

Suppose the HTML contains:

<body>
  <h1>Hello</h1>

  <script src="app.js"></script>

  <p>More content</p>
</body>

With a classic script like this, the HTML parser reaches the script and, by default, parser-blocking behavior occurs.

Conceptually:

HTML parser
    │
    │ reaches <script>
    ▼
stop normal parsing
    │
    ▼
obtain JavaScript source
    │
    ▼
execute the script
    │
    ▼
resume parsing

This means the parser does not simply race ahead as though the script did not exist.

That is a very important runtime interaction: HTML parsing and JavaScript execution are coupled by default for classic scripts.

11. Why would the browser ever need to stop parsing for JavaScript?

This behavior looks surprising until you remember that JavaScript can interact with the document while parsing is taking place.

Historically, a classic script could use APIs such as:

document.write("<p>hello</p>");

which can inject markup at the parser's current insertion point.

That means the parser cannot always assume:

“I know exactly what the document will look like later, so I can safely run ahead.”

JavaScript can participate in construction of the document itself.

You do not need to use document.write() in modern applications to understand the historical reason for parser blocking. The important lesson is that web-platform behavior often has to preserve old semantics, even when newer coding styles would prefer a cleaner model.

12. Why a script in <head> can make the page feel blank

Suppose a large synchronous script is encountered near the beginning of the document.

<head>
  <script src="huge.js"></script>
</head>

The parser can be blocked before it has constructed much of the body.

So the user may see very little useful page content while the script is downloading and executing.

This is not because JavaScript “turns the screen white.” It is because the browser's document construction has not progressed to the point where the content the user cares about can be fully constructed and rendered.

13. defer: download now, execute after parsing

The defer attribute changes the timing relationship.

<script src="app.js" defer></script>

The important mental model is:

HTML parsing ─────────────────────► complete
       │
       │ script downloads in parallel
       ▼
script execution                ► after parsing

For classic external scripts, deferred scripts execute after the document has been parsed, and they preserve their document order.

So:

<script src="a.js" defer></script>
<script src="b.js" defer></script>

preserves the intended script order even though the files can download in parallel.

This makes defer particularly useful for application code that expects the HTML to exist by the time it starts.

14. async: download in parallel, run when ready

async makes a different promise:

<script src="analytics.js" async></script>

The browser can download the script without waiting for parsing to finish, but once the script is ready it can execute immediately.

HTML parsing ───────────────────────────►

script download ───────────► ready
                              │
                              ▼
                           execute

That execution can happen while parsing is still in progress.

And unlike deferred scripts, multiple async scripts do not promise document-order execution.

So the useful comparison is:

Classic defaultdeferasync
Blocks parser, then executesDownloads in parallel, executes after parsingDownloads in parallel, executes as soon as ready
Strong ordering by parser positionPreserves document orderNo reliable ordering between independent async scripts

15. Modules change the mental model again

A module script:

<script type="module" src="app.js"></script>

has module semantics and is deferred by default.

It also participates in the language's module system:

import { render } from "./render.js";
export function start() {
  ...
}

The browser resolves module dependencies through URLs, fetches them, builds the module dependency graph, and evaluates modules according to module semantics rather than treating every script as one unrelated classic script.

For your mental model, the important point at this node is not to memorise every module loading rule. It is:

“script execution” is not one single mechanism. Classic scripts and module scripts have different loading/evaluation semantics.

16. When the JavaScript finally runs, it already has a world around it

Now return to Node 0.

We said the host environment gives the JavaScript program browser capabilities.

That is visible when the engine begins executing top-level code.

console.log(location.href);
document.title = "Hello";
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("later");
}, 1000);

Where did those names come from?

They were not introduced by your source file.

The browser created a JavaScript execution environment in which those browser-provided capabilities are available.

That is the bridge from:

browser host
     ↓
JavaScript execution environment
     ↓
your code

17. The global object explains why browser APIs seem to be “everywhere”

This is the place where your recent global-object discovery becomes concrete.

In a classic browser page there is a global object exposed through window.

window
 ├── document
 ├── location
 ├── navigator
 ├── console
 ├── localStorage
 ├── fetch
 ├── setTimeout
 └── ...

Again, this is a conceptual picture, not a literal source-level object literal representing the entire browser.

The important thing is that the global environment gives your code access to a set of globally available bindings and host-provided objects/functions.

That is why you can write:

document.querySelector("#app");

without first declaring:

const document = ...;

The browser has already established the global environment in which the name can be resolved.

18. Why document is not a magic keyword

This is one of the most useful debugging facts to internalize.

document is not like:

if
for
return
const

Those are language syntax.

document is a name available in the browser's global environment.

That is why code can meaningfully distinguish:

typeof document

across hosts.

In a normal browser page, you get a browser-provided value representing the page's document. In a host that has no page DOM, there may be no such binding.

The JavaScript language did not change. The host environment changed.

That is the same language-vs-host distinction from Node 0, now expressed through an actual browser object.

19. DOMContentLoaded and load mark different points in the page lifecycle

Two events are particularly useful for understanding when the document has reached important milestones.

DOMContentLoaded means that the HTML document has been fully parsed, and deferred/module scripts that must complete before it have been evaluated according to their loading semantics.

HTML parsing complete
        ↓
DOMContentLoaded

This is why application code often uses it when it needs the document structure to exist.

load is later. It waits for the page's dependent subresources such as images and other load-blocking resources to reach their loaded state.

HTML parsed
   ↓
DOMContentLoaded
   ↓
other page resources finish
   ↓
load

Do not memorise this as “DOMContentLoaded = everything is loaded.” That is too strong.

Instead:

DOMContentLoaded is primarily about the document having been parsed; load is about the broader page load reaching completion.

20. What you can explain after Node 1 — and what Node 1 intentionally leaves broken

At this point you should be able to tell the complete story at a high level:

1. The user navigates to a URL.
2. The browser obtains the referenced resource.
3. The response arrives as bytes.
4. For an HTML document, those bytes are decoded and parsed.
5. Parsing constructs a live DOM/document representation.
6. The parser encounters scripts according to their loading semantics.
7. JavaScript source is obtained and handed to the JavaScript engine.
8. The engine executes that source inside a browser-provided environment.
9. Browser-provided globals such as document, window, fetch and timers are available.
10. DOMContentLoaded marks an important “document parsed” milestone.

And you should now be able to answer the conceptual question that caused so much earlier confusion:

The HTML is the textual input. The DOM is the browser-created object model derived from that input. document is the JavaScript-visible object representing that live document model. The browser then executes JavaScript against that environment.

But there is still a precise gap.

Your JavaScript can now run. The document can now exist. But the program runs top-to-bottom and then reaches the end.

The user has not clicked anything yet.

Nothing explains how the browser can later say:

“Hey — that click just happened.
Run this function you gave me earlier.”

What's still broken: the browser can start your program, but we have not yet explained how it calls your program back later in response to events. That is the problem Node 2 exists to solve.

sections.title: Node 2 — The runtime calls you back
sections.content:
What this node is trying to establish: Node 1 explained how a page becomes a running JavaScript program and deliberately stopped at the moment the program reaches the end. But a browser page does not become inert when your top-level script finishes. The user can click, type, move a pointer, resize a window, submit a form, or trigger other browser events later. Node 2 explains the mechanism that turns those future happenings into calls back into your JavaScript: event listeners, callbacks, event objects, propagation, and the basic “browser calls you later” model.

The single most useful mental model for this node is:

your program starts
      ↓
register a callback
      ↓
your current code finishes
      ↓
time passes
      ↓
something happens in the browser
      ↓
browser dispatches an event
      ↓
browser finds the relevant listeners
      ↓
browser calls your callback
      ↓
your JavaScript runs again

That is the inversion that this node introduces: you do not repeatedly ask the browser whether something happened; you give the browser code to call when it does.

1. Start with the limitation Node 1 left behind

Node 1 ended with a program that can start and interact with the current document, but whose top-level execution eventually reaches the end.

Imagine:

console.log("page loaded");

The engine evaluates the statement, prints the message, and eventually reaches the end of the current script.

But the page is still alive. Five seconds later the user might click a button.

So there is an obvious unanswered question:

How can JavaScript that has already finished running do something later?

The answer is not that the same top-level code somehow stays suspended forever. The answer is that your program can register functions with the host and the host can later call those functions.

2. The fundamental pattern is “give me a function to call later”

Suppose you have:

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick);

The important part is handleClick.

You are not calling it here.

handleClick()

would mean “execute this function right now.”

Instead:

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick);

means, conceptually:

“Browser, remember this function and call it when a click event is dispatched for this target.”

That is the callback model.

Your code runs now to establish the relationship. The callback runs later when the relevant event occurs.

3. addEventListener is a method on an EventTarget

When you write:

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick);

the dots matter.

button is a JavaScript-visible object representing the DOM element. addEventListener is a method associated with the EventTarget interface.

Conceptually:

button
   ↓
access "addEventListener"
   ↓
function-valued method
   ↓
call it with:
   "click"
   handleClick

This connects directly to your object-model understanding from Node 0. There is no new mysterious syntax here. It is still property access followed by a function call.

The browser implementation behind that object is maintaining listener registrations and knows what to do when an event is later dispatched.

4. What exactly gets stored when you register a listener?

A useful conceptual model is that the event target maintains a collection of listener registrations.

button
  │
  └── event listener list
       │
       ├── "click" → handleClick
       ├── "mouseover" → handleHover
       └── "keydown" → handleKey

This is a mental model, not a claim about the browser's exact internal memory layout.

The important idea is identity: the browser needs to know which function is associated with which event type and under which listener options.

That is also why function identity matters later when removing a listener.

5. Calling the method is immediate; calling the callback is not

This distinction is extremely important.

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick);

The addEventListener method runs immediately while your current JavaScript is executing.

The handleClick callback normally does not run at that moment.

Later:

user clicks button
       ↓
browser dispatches click event
       ↓
browser invokes handleClick

So the registration operation and the future callback invocation are two different executions separated by time.

6. An event is the browser saying “something happened”

An event is a browser/platform-defined occurrence or notification that can be dispatched to interested objects.

Examples include:

click
keydown
input
submit
pointermove
resize
load
DOMContentLoaded

The event is not itself your function. It is the thing that causes the browser to decide that certain listeners should run.

Conceptually:

occurrence
   ↓
event object / event dispatch
   ↓
matching listeners
   ↓
callbacks execute

This is why “event” and “callback” should never be treated as synonyms.

7. The event object is the information packet for that occurrence

When the browser invokes a listener, it normally supplies an event object:

button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log(event);
});

The event object contains information about the occurrence and its propagation.

Depending on the event type and API, it can expose things such as:

event.type
event.target
event.currentTarget
event.bubbles
event.cancelable
event.defaultPrevented
event.eventPhase

Think of it as the browser handing your callback a structured description of the event currently being dispatched.

8. target and currentTarget are not the same concept

This is one of the most important distinctions to internalize.

<div id="card">
  <button id="save">Save</button>
</div>

Suppose the listener is attached to the div:

card.addEventListener("click", handler);

and the user clicks the button.

Then:

event.target
    ↓
the button where the event originated

event.currentTarget
    ↓
the div whose listener is currently executing

The event can travel through multiple elements. The target remains the original event target, while currentTarget identifies the listener's current target during that invocation. This distinction is fundamental to event delegation.

9. Why can one click involve many elements?

Because DOM elements are nested.

window
  ↓
document
  ↓
body
  ↓
div
  ↓
button
  ↓
span

If an event occurs on the span, the browser has a propagation path through the relevant ancestor chain.

The browser does not simply say:

“The span was clicked, therefore only the span gets a chance.”

Instead, event dispatch has defined propagation phases.

10. Capture: the event travels downward toward the target

The first phase is capturing.

Conceptually:

window
   ↓
document
   ↓
body
   ↓
div
   ↓
button
   ↓
target

Listeners registered with the capture option can run as the event travels downward.

container.addEventListener(
  "click",
  handler,
  { capture: true }
);

Most ordinary listeners do not use capture explicitly. By default, addEventListener() registers a listener for the bubbling phase.

11. Target: the event reaches the thing that was actually targeted

Eventually the propagation path reaches the event's target.

If the user actually clicked the button:

<button>Save</button>

that button is the event target.

This is commonly where you conceptually think “the click happened,” but remember that the dispatch process has already been defined in terms of a path and phases.

The exact listener behavior at the target can involve listeners registered with or without capture, according to the event dispatch rules.

12. Bubble: the event travels back upward

After the target phase, events that are configured to bubble can travel back up the ancestor chain.

target
   ↑
button
   ↑
div
   ↑
body
   ↑
document
   ↑
window

This is why a listener on a parent can respond to an event that actually originated from a child.

For a normal listener:

parent.addEventListener("click", handler);

a click on a descendant can reach handler during bubbling.

Capture and bubbling are not two different kinds of events. They are phases of event propagation.

13. Event delegation is just using bubbling deliberately

Consider a list with one hundred buttons:

<ul id="items">
  <li><button>One</button></li>
  <li><button>Two</button></li>
  ...
</ul>

You could attach one listener to every button.

Or you can attach one listener to the parent:

items.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest("button");
  if (!button) return;

  // handle the clicked button
});

The browser lets the event bubble from the clicked child to the parent.

The parent inspects event.target to determine what actually originated the event.

That is event delegation: one listener handles events originating from many descendants.

It is especially useful when descendants can be created dynamically after the listener was registered.

14. preventDefault and stopPropagation solve different problems

Suppose a link was clicked:

<a href="/dashboard">Dashboard</a>

The browser may have a default action: navigate to the referenced URL.

Your handler can say:

event.preventDefault();

That means “do not perform the event's default action, if it is cancelable.”

That is different from:

event.stopPropagation();

which means “do not continue propagating this event through the capture/bubble path.”

Stopping propagation does not itself cancel the browser's default action. Conversely, preventing the default does not stop the event from travelling through other listeners.

15. stopImmediatePropagation is even stronger

Imagine the same element has multiple listeners for the same event.

button.addEventListener("click", first);
button.addEventListener("click", second);

stopPropagation() stops propagation to other elements, but it does not necessarily prevent remaining listeners on the current element from running.

stopImmediatePropagation() is stronger: it prevents the remaining listeners for that event from being invoked as well.

That distinction is useful when debugging code where “the event still ran another handler” seems mysterious.

16. A listener is a registration with options, not just a function

The third argument to addEventListener() can specify behavior.

element.addEventListener(
  "click",
  handler,
  {
    capture: true,
    once: true,
    passive: true
  }
);

Common options include:

OptionMeaning
captureRun during the capture phase
onceAutomatically remove the listener after its first invocation
passivePromise not to call preventDefault()
signalAssociate the listener with an AbortSignal so it can be removed by aborting

These options reinforce an important point: the browser is maintaining structured listener registrations, not merely a vague “list of functions.”

17. Why function identity matters when removing a listener

Suppose:

button.addEventListener("click", handler);
button.removeEventListener("click", handler);

The browser can identify the registered listener because handler refers to the same function object.

Compare:

button.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("hi"));

button.removeEventListener(
  "click",
  () => console.log("hi")
);

Those two arrow-function expressions create distinct function objects. They look textually identical, but they are not the same function identity.

This is another direct application of the JavaScript object model: functions are values and have identity, so registration APIs can distinguish one function object from another.

18. The browser can call your function long after your original script finished

This is where the callback model becomes conceptually powerful.

button.addEventListener("click", handleClick);

console.log("top-level script finished");

The top-level script can finish completely.

Then:

10 seconds later...

user clicks
      ↓
browser dispatches click
      ↓
browser invokes handleClick
      ↓
handleClick runs as a new piece of JavaScript execution

There is no contradiction between “the script finished” and “the function runs later.” They are separate invocations of JavaScript associated with different moments in the host's lifetime.

This is the first place where you should start thinking of your application not as one top-to-bottom program, but as a program that registers future work with the host.

19. JavaScript itself still runs synchronously once the callback starts

Do not accidentally conclude that callbacks make JavaScript parallel.

Suppose:

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log("A");
  doExpensiveWork();
  console.log("B");
});

Once this callback starts executing, ordinary JavaScript execution proceeds synchronously.

The browser does not normally pause the callback halfway through and run another JavaScript callback in the same execution context at the same time.

So callback-based event handling gives you time separation, not simultaneous JavaScript execution.

callback starts
    ↓
A
    ↓
expensive work
    ↓
B
    ↓
callback ends

This observation will become crucial when we study the event loop and why a long-running callback can freeze the page.

20. What you can explain after Node 2 — and what Node 2 intentionally leaves broken

You should now be able to explain the entire callback/event picture:

1. Your initial JavaScript executes.
2. It registers a listener using addEventListener().
3. The listener registration records an event type, callback and options.
4. Your current JavaScript execution eventually finishes.
5. A browser event occurs later.
6. The browser dispatches the event.
7. The event follows a propagation path.
8. Capture listeners can run on the way down.
9. Target listeners run at the target.
10. Bubbling listeners can run on the way back up.
11. The browser supplies an event object to each listener.
12. The listener callback runs synchronously to completion.

And the key mental model should now be:

The browser owns the event source and dispatch machinery. Your JavaScript supplies callbacks. When an event occurs, the browser dispatches it through the DOM event system and invokes the callbacks that were registered for that event.

You should also now be able to distinguish:

event
    ≠ callback

target
    ≠ currentTarget

preventDefault()
    ≠ stopPropagation()

stopPropagation()
    ≠ stopImmediatePropagation()

register callback
    ≠ call callback

But there is still a precise gap.

We have said that the browser can receive events, determine the appropriate listeners, and call JavaScript.

We have not yet explained what happens when multiple things become ready to run at roughly the same time.

What happens if:

a click happens
while another callback is running?

a timer becomes ready
while a network response arrives?

two user actions happen quickly?

a callback takes 500 ms?

Who decides what runs next?

Where is the queue?

When exactly does the browser get another chance to run JavaScript?

What's still broken: we have explained the mechanism by which the browser can call you back, but not the machinery that decides when queued work gets its turn on the JavaScript thread. That is the problem Node 3/Node 4 will progressively unpack, beginning with what the browser actually is as a collection of processes and threads and then reaching the event loop itself.

sections.title: Node 3 — What the browser actually is, as a set of running programs
sections.content:
'

What this node is trying to establish: Node 2 explained how the browser can call your JavaScript back when something happens. That leaves the next question: what else is running while your callback runs, and what exactly does “the browser is running my JavaScript” mean at the operating-system level? This node builds the process/thread model first, then connects it to the browser's renderer architecture and to the crucial fact that a normal page's JavaScript shares an execution thread with other work on that page.

The single most useful mental model for this node is:

Browser
  │
  ├── browser process
  ├── renderer process(es)
  │      ├── JavaScript engine
  │      ├── DOM
  │      ├── style/layout
  │      ├── event dispatch
  │      └── page JavaScript on a main thread
  │
  ├── GPU process / rendering support
  ├── network-related services
  └── other isolated processes

Do not treat that diagram as one universal process layout for every browser and every version. It is a conceptual architecture. The important thing is that “the browser” is not one giant JavaScript process with one giant thread.

1. Start with the limitation Node 2 left behind

Node 2 established that the browser can register your callback and invoke it later. But that phrase hides an enormous question:

What is the thing that is actually running all this work?

If your click handler is executing, are timers also executing at exactly the same time? Is another tab executing in the same thread? Can another callback enter the same JavaScript object halfway through your function? What does it mean for a tab to “freeze”?

To answer those questions, we need two operating-system concepts: process and thread.

2. A process is an isolated running program environment

A process is a running program together with resources and, crucially, an address-space boundary that separates it from other processes.

Conceptually:

Process A
  memory A

Process B
  memory B

Ordinarily, code in Process A cannot simply dereference an address in Process B's memory and start changing it. The operating system enforces isolation.

This isolation gives us an important failure boundary.

If one renderer process crashes, the operating system can terminate that process without necessarily terminating the entire browser application.

So when somebody says “Chrome has many processes,” the important meaning is not just “there are many programs.” It is that browser components are deliberately given separate isolation domains.

3. A thread is one sequence of execution inside a process

A thread is an execution context inside a process.

The simplest mental model is:

Process
  │
  ├── Thread A
  ├── Thread B
  └── Thread C

Threads belonging to the same process share that process's address space.

That makes communication between threads potentially much cheaper than communication between isolated processes, because threads can access shared memory.

But shared memory creates a different class of problems: two threads can potentially access the same state at overlapping times, which introduces races, synchronization requirements, locks, atomics, and other concurrency concerns.

You do not need all of those mechanisms yet. The key vocabulary is:

Processes provide stronger isolation; threads provide multiple execution sequences inside a shared process memory space.

4. Process versus thread: the distinction in one picture

Operating system
│
├── Process A
│    ├── Thread A1
│    └── Thread A2
│
└── Process B
     ├── Thread B1
     └── Thread B2

Process A and Process B are isolated memory domains.

A1 and A2 share Process A's memory.

B1 and B2 share Process B's memory.

This gives you two different ways of structuring work:

process boundary → isolation
thread boundary  → parallel execution inside shared memory

That distinction will matter enormously when we later discuss browser security and Web Workers.

5. Why would a browser use multiple processes?

A browser executes untrusted code from many different websites. Giving every page unrestricted access to one common process would be an enormous security and reliability problem.

Separate processes provide containment.

Conceptually:

Site A
   ↓
isolated renderer process

Site B
   ↓
isolated renderer process

If Site A's rendering code crashes, Site B should not automatically crash with it.

More importantly, a vulnerability that gives an attacker code execution inside a renderer process is more useful to an attacker if that process has broad access to the machine. Modern browsers therefore combine process isolation with sandboxing and other security boundaries.

So multi-process architecture is not primarily about making JavaScript faster. It is heavily about reliability, isolation, and security.

6. “The browser” is therefore an architectural collection, not one thing

When developers say “the browser does X,” that phrase can hide many components.

A useful conceptual split is:

Browser application
│
├── browser/UI responsibilities
│    ├── tabs
│    ├── address bar
│    └── window management
│
├── content/rendering responsibilities
│    ├── HTML parsing
│    ├── DOM
│    ├── CSS/style processing
│    ├── layout
│    ├── JavaScript
│    └── painting
│
├── graphics/GPU responsibilities
│
├── networking responsibilities
│
└── other services / isolated components

The exact decomposition differs between browser engines and implementations, but the architectural lesson is stable: the browser is a system, not a single JavaScript runtime box.

7. Where does the JavaScript engine fit?

Return to Node 0's distinction.

Your JavaScript
      ↓
JavaScript engine
      ↓
host environment

Now make the host more concrete:

Browser renderer
      │
      ├── JavaScript engine
      ├── DOM
      ├── event system
      ├── rendering/style/layout
      └── scheduling machinery

The JavaScript engine is one component inside this larger environment.

That means V8, for example, is not itself “the browser runtime.” It is the JavaScript engine embedded by a host that surrounds it with other capabilities.

8. The main thread: the thread your page's JavaScript normally executes on

For ordinary page JavaScript, the most important execution context is the main thread.

A useful conceptual picture is:

Renderer process
      │
      └── main thread
            ├── JavaScript
            ├── DOM operations
            ├── event dispatch
            ├── style/layout work
            └── other page-facing work

The exact internal division of rendering work is implementation-specific, and modern browsers use additional threads for many tasks. But for learning browser JavaScript, the main-thread model is crucial:

your ordinary page JavaScript runs in an execution context that is also responsible for important parts of the page's interactive work.

9. Why “one main thread” is such a powerful fact

Suppose this callback runs:

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  for (;;) {}
});

That infinite loop is not merely “making JavaScript busy.” It occupies the page's JavaScript execution thread indefinitely.

As a result, the browser cannot keep progressing through ordinary main-thread work for that page.

The practical symptom is a frozen page.

JavaScript callback starts
        ↓
main thread occupied
        ↓
other main-thread work waits
        ↓
UI becomes unresponsive

This is the beginning of the explanation for browser jank and freezing.

10. JavaScript callbacks are not interrupted halfway through by another callback

This is a major simplifying property of the ordinary page execution model.

Consider:

function first() {
  console.log("A");
  doLotsOfWork();
  console.log("B");
}

function second() {
  console.log("C");
}

If first() is currently executing on the page's JavaScript execution thread, another ordinary JavaScript callback does not simply enter the same execution context halfway through first().

Conceptually:

first()
  A
  lots of work
  B
  ↓
first finishes

then another callback can run

This gives ordinary JavaScript a useful form of run-to-completion behavior.

It means you do not normally need a mutex just to protect a JavaScript object from another callback simultaneously executing against that same object in the same event-loop turn.

11. Then why does a page freeze instead of doing something else?

Because the same simplification that prevents two ordinary callbacks from simultaneously mutating the same page state also creates the single-thread bottleneck.

If your callback takes:

5 ms

the delay is usually unnoticeable.

If it takes:

500 ms

the browser has half a second during which other main-thread work cannot receive its turn.

If it takes:

5000 ms

the page can feel completely frozen.

This gives you a first-principles explanation for the advice:

Do not block the main thread with long-running JavaScript.

12. “But aren't there other browser threads?”

Yes.

Modern browsers use multiple threads for many tasks: networking, image decoding, compositor work, browser services, workers, and implementation-specific background work are examples.

But that does not mean your normal page JavaScript automatically runs in parallel with itself.

The crucial distinction is:

Browser has many threads
        ≠
your page's ordinary JavaScript executes simultaneously on many threads

JavaScript running in the normal page execution context remains associated with its designated execution thread.

13. The DOM is not simply “shared memory that every thread can touch”

This is another place where intuition can go wrong.

You might hear:

“The browser has many threads, so why can't two threads modify the DOM at once?”

The browser deliberately avoids exposing the ordinary page DOM as an arbitrary multi-threaded shared-memory data structure.

Instead, the standard page DOM is associated with a particular execution context, and ordinary page JavaScript interacts with it through that context.

When the browser provides true parallel JavaScript through Web Workers, those workers do not simply receive unrestricted access to the same page DOM.

That restriction is not accidental. It avoids a huge class of races such as:

Thread A
  reads child list

Thread B
  removes child

Thread A
  continues using stale assumption

Instead, the browser gives worker code different communication primitives, which we will study later.

14. A useful mental model of a renderer process

             RENDERER PROCESS
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                          │
│  Main thread                             │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ JavaScript engine                  │  │
│  │ DOM / document                    │  │
│  │ event dispatch                    │  │
│  │ style/layout work                 │  │
│  │ page script execution             │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                          │
│  Other renderer threads                  │
│  ├── implementation-specific work        │
│  ├── decoding / parsing helpers          │
│  ├── compositor-related work             │
│  └── workers                             │
│                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

Again, this is a conceptual model rather than a literal thread dump from one browser version.

The point is to stop thinking:

browser
  └── JavaScript

and start thinking:

browser system
  └── renderer environment
        └── execution contexts
              └── ordinary page JavaScript on a main thread

15. Process isolation also explains why tabs can fail independently

Imagine two sites:

Site A → renderer process A
Site B → renderer process B

If renderer A crashes, renderer B can continue.

This is one of the major user-facing benefits of browser isolation.

The same principle becomes even more important when you consider untrusted web content. A browser does not want arbitrary JavaScript from a webpage to have the same privileges as the browser's own privileged UI code.

Therefore, process isolation and sandboxing form part of the security architecture surrounding JavaScript execution.

16. What “shared memory” means for threads, and why it matters later

Threads inside one process can access the same process memory.

That sounds convenient:

Thread A ──┐
           ├── shared process memory
Thread B ──┘

But shared memory means the program must deal with possible conflicting access.

For example:

sharedCounter = 0

Thread A: read 0
Thread B: read 0
Thread A: write 1
Thread B: write 1

Two increments have happened conceptually, but the final value can still be 1 because the two operations overlapped.

This is the sort of race that multi-threaded systems must explicitly handle.

Ordinary page JavaScript avoids this particular class of problem by not exposing the page's main DOM programming model as arbitrary simultaneous multi-threaded access.

17. Web Workers are not “another copy of the same DOM thread”

Later we will study workers properly, but this node needs one boundary.

A Web Worker gives JavaScript another execution context that can run independently of the page's normal main-thread execution.

Page
  │
  ├── Main-thread JavaScript
  │
  └── Worker JavaScript
          │
          └── no normal direct page-DOM access

The two contexts communicate through messaging.

Main thread
    │
    │ postMessage(...)
    ▼
Worker
    │
    │ postMessage(...)
    ▼
Main thread

This is fundamentally different from “two callbacks now run inside the same page object graph at the same time.”

18. Why process/thread vocabulary is necessary before the event loop

We can now state the question that Node 4 or the next event-loop node needs to answer much more precisely.

We know:

browser
  ↓
renderer environment
  ↓
main execution thread
  ↓
JavaScript callbacks

We also know:

many things can happen:
  user input
  timers
  network activity
  rendering work
  promise reactions

But the main JavaScript execution context cannot simply run all of those simultaneously.

Therefore something must decide:

which ready piece of JavaScript gets the main thread next?

That question is much easier to understand once you know what a process and thread are.

19. The complete browser execution picture so far

Operating system
       │
       ▼
Browser processes
       │
       ├── Browser/UI process
       │
       ├── Renderer process
       │      │
       │      └── Main thread
       │             │
       │             ├── JavaScript engine
       │             ├── DOM
       │             ├── Event system
       │             ├── Style/layout
       │             └── Page JavaScript
       │
       ├── Other renderer / worker contexts
       ├── GPU-related process
       └── Other browser services

Your JavaScript does not float above the operating system in a magical “browser layer.” It runs inside a concrete execution environment that ultimately runs as threads inside operating-system processes.

At the same time, you should not over-literalize the picture. Browser implementations are complex, distributed systems, and many operations cross process boundaries or use internal services. The purpose of the diagram is to establish the right levels of abstraction.

20. What you can explain after Node 3 — and what Node 3 intentionally leaves broken

You should now be able to explain:

process
    = isolation boundary / running program environment

thread
    = execution sequence inside a process

browser
    = a multi-component system using processes and threads

renderer
    = environment responsible for page/content work

main thread
    = the primary execution context for ordinary page JavaScript

JavaScript callback
    = code that runs when the browser gives the main execution
      context its turn

You should also be able to explain why this is true:

A page can have many things happening around it, yet its ordinary JavaScript callbacks do not all execute simultaneously on the same page execution context.

And you should understand why a long-running callback causes a freeze:

long callback
     ↓
main execution thread occupied
     ↓
other main-thread work waits
     ↓
page stops responding normally

But we still have the central unanswered question.

Node 2 told us that events can cause callbacks to become runnable.

Node 3 told us that ordinary page JavaScript ultimately needs a main execution thread.

Now we need the missing machinery between those two facts:

event / timer / network completion / other source
                         ↓
                 work becomes ready
                         ↓
                       ????
                         ↓
                 main thread runs it

Who chooses the next callback?

Where are ready tasks represented?

What is the difference between a task and a microtask?

When does the browser render between pieces of JavaScript?

Why does Promise.then() often run before a timer, even when the timer was registered first?

Why does setTimeout(fn, 0) not mean “run this immediately”?

What's still broken: we now know the physical execution setting — processes, threads, renderer, and main-thread JavaScript — but not the scheduling mechanism that decides what gets to execute next. That is the problem the event-loop node exists to solve.

'

sections.title: Node 4 — The event loop
sections.content:
'

What this node is trying to establish: Node 2 gave us the callback model: the browser can call your function later. Node 3 gave us the physical execution setting: ordinary page JavaScript runs on a main execution thread, and that thread cannot execute two ordinary JavaScript callbacks simultaneously. The missing piece is the scheduler between those facts. Node 4 builds the event-loop mental model: work becomes ready, gets queued into the browser's scheduling machinery, and eventually gets a turn on the main thread.

The single most useful mental model for this node is:

browser / host work happens
        ↓
some JavaScript work becomes runnable
        ↓
it is placed into the appropriate scheduling queue
        ↓
the main JavaScript execution context becomes available
        ↓
the browser chooses what runs next
        ↓
callback runs to completion
        ↓
browser gets another scheduling point

This node is where phrases such as task, queue, microtask, event loop, timer, and rendering opportunity stop being loose vocabulary and become parts of one coherent model.

1. Start with the exact limitation Node 3 left behind

We now know something is producing runnable JavaScript work.

A user can click. A timer can become ready. A network operation can complete. A promise reaction can become ready. A browser-controlled lifecycle event can fire.

But the page still has one ordinary JavaScript execution thread.

So there is a scheduling problem:

When several pieces of work are ready, which one gets the main thread next?

This is the problem the event loop exists to help us reason about.

2. “The event loop” is a scheduling model, not a little JavaScript loop running forever

Beginners often imagine something like:

while (true) {
  checkQueue();
  runNextCallback();
}

That picture is useful as a first approximation, but dangerous if you take it literally.

The event loop is a host-level scheduling concept that coordinates execution of JavaScript jobs/tasks with other browser work. The browser is doing many things outside JavaScript, and the event loop is part of the machinery that determines when JavaScript gets another opportunity to execute.

So do not imagine “the event loop” as a JavaScript function in your source code.

Think instead:

The host owns scheduling; JavaScript is one kind of work that gets scheduled onto an execution context.

3. A queue is not “a magical list where everything goes”

The word queue is used very loosely in tutorials.

In browser scheduling there are different categories of scheduled work with different semantics. Calling all of them simply “the callback queue” loses important information.

A useful simplified picture is:

events / timers / other task sources
              ↓
         task scheduling

promise reactions / mutation observers
              ↓
          microtasks

browser rendering work
              ↓
       rendering opportunities

The exact standards terminology is more detailed than this, but the separation is essential.

4. What is a task?

A task is a unit of work that the browser can schedule for execution as part of its event-loop processing model.

Examples of things that can lead to tasks include user interaction events, timer callbacks, and other host-specified sources of runnable work.

The useful mental model is:

source of activity
      ↓
task becomes ready
      ↓
event-loop scheduling
      ↓
JavaScript callback eventually runs

Do not equate:

task = event
task = function
task = queue

These are different concepts.

5. What happens when a click occurs?

Return to Node 2.

user clicks button
       ↓
browser determines the event
       ↓
event is dispatched
       ↓
matching listeners are found
       ↓
a piece of runnable work is scheduled
       ↓
main JavaScript execution gets a turn
       ↓
listener callback executes

The important thing is that “the user clicked” and “the callback is currently executing” are not necessarily the same instant.

There is host-side machinery between the physical/browser event and the JavaScript execution of your callback.

6. Why setTimeout(fn, 0) does not mean “run fn now”

This is one of the classic misconceptions.

setTimeout(fn, 0);

does not mean:

“Interrupt the current JavaScript and execute fn immediately.”

It means, conceptually:

“Make this timer callback eligible to be scheduled after the timer's required delay rules, then let the event-loop machinery determine when it can execute.”

If JavaScript is already running:

console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("B");
}, 0);

console.log("C");

the ordinary result is:

A
C
B

because the current JavaScript execution must complete before another task can take the main execution thread.

7. A timer is not a sleeping JavaScript thread

Another useful correction:

setTimeout(fn, 1000);

does not normally mean that the JavaScript engine creates a thread, puts that thread to sleep for one second, and then wakes it up inside the same call stack.

The timer is a host scheduling facility.

JavaScript
   │
   ├── registers timer
   │
   └── continues executing

host timer machinery
   │
   └── waits for the relevant time condition

timer becomes eligible
   │
   └── callback can later be scheduled

The callback still has to wait for the main JavaScript execution context to become available.

8. The current callback has to finish before the next ordinary callback can run

Consider:

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  console.log("start");

  const end = performance.now() + 500;
  while (performance.now() < end) {}

  console.log("end");
});

During that half-second of synchronous execution, the browser cannot simply pause this callback halfway through and begin another ordinary page callback in the same execution context.

So if another event becomes ready:

callback A is running
       │
       ├── event B occurs
       │
       └── B waits for its turn

callback A finishes
       ↓
scheduler can choose another piece of work

This is the practical meaning of JavaScript's run-to-completion model in the normal page execution context.

9. Microtasks are a different category of scheduled work

Now we reach the distinction that explains much of modern JavaScript behavior.

A microtask is a unit of work that is processed at a microtask checkpoint, with promise reactions and mutation-observer callbacks being important examples.

Suppose:

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("promise");
});

The callback is not simply placed into the same scheduling category as a timer task.

Conceptually:

Promise reaction
      ↓
microtask queue
      ↓
microtask checkpoint
      ↓
callback runs

This distinction is essential for predicting output ordering.

10. The classic task-versus-microtask example

console.log("A");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("timer");
}, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("promise");
});

console.log("B");

The useful simplified ordering is:

A
B
promise
timer

Why?

First, the current script runs synchronously:

A
B

Then, after the current task reaches a microtask checkpoint, the promise reaction runs.

Only later does a timer task get its turn.

This is why the phrase “everything goes into one callback queue” is not sufficient for understanding browser scheduling.

11. What is a microtask checkpoint?

A microtask checkpoint is a scheduling point at which the host processes the pending microtask queue.

The important behavior to internalize is:

current JavaScript task runs
        ↓
task reaches a microtask checkpoint
        ↓
microtasks are drained
        ↓
browser can proceed to later event-loop work

If processing one microtask adds another microtask:

queue:
  microtask A

run A
  ↓
A queues B

queue:
  microtask B

run B
  ↓
...

the microtask queue keeps being processed until the checkpoint is exhausted according to the scheduling rules.

This is why repeatedly generating microtasks can delay other work.

12. Microtasks can therefore starve tasks

Imagine code that continually queues another microtask:

function again() {
  queueMicrotask(again);
}
