queueMicrotask(again);

This creates an effectively endless stream of microtasks.

The danger is that the browser can spend its scheduling time draining microtasks rather than reaching later task or rendering opportunities.

microtask
   ↓
queues microtask
   ↓
microtask
   ↓
queues microtask
   ↓
...

So “microtasks are faster” is not the right mental model.

The better statement is:

Microtasks have stronger scheduling priority within the event-loop model, and that priority can become a problem if you continually generate more work.

13. queueMicrotask versus Promise.then

Both can be used to schedule microtask work:

queueMicrotask(() => {
  console.log("microtask");
});

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("promise reaction");
});

For the scheduling model at this level, the important commonality is that they participate in the microtask mechanism rather than becoming ordinary timer tasks.

The practical difference is mainly in how the work is expressed and what semantic/error-handling behavior surrounds the callback.

Do not create a false hierarchy such as:

queueMicrotask = “more asynchronous”
Promise.then = “less asynchronous”

They are both ways of arranging microtask work.

14. Why Promise callbacks can run before a timer registered earlier

This is now straightforward.

setTimeout(timer, 0);

Promise.resolve().then(promiseCallback);

The timer registration and promise registration happen during the same synchronous execution.

But they enter different scheduling mechanisms.

timer
  → task scheduling

promise reaction
  → microtask queue

After the current script completes, the microtask checkpoint gets processed before the scheduler moves on to later task work.

So “registered first” does not imply “runs first” when work belongs to different scheduling categories.

15. Where does rendering fit?

This is where the browser diverges from the simplistic “event loop = callback queue” story.

The browser also has to keep the visible page up to date.

Conceptually:

JavaScript work
     ↓
microtask processing
     ↓
possible rendering opportunity
     ↓
next scheduled work

The exact rendering algorithm is more complicated and browser-dependent, and rendering is not guaranteed after every callback.

The important point is:

The browser is scheduling more than JavaScript. It also has to coordinate rendering and other browser work.

16. Why a tiny callback can still affect rendering

Imagine:

for (let i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) {
  updateSomething();
}

Even if each operation is individually tiny, the entire synchronous callback is one uninterrupted piece of main-thread work.

The browser cannot necessarily paint intermediate states simply because your code changed the DOM repeatedly.

Conceptually:

callback starts
  ↓
DOM mutation
  ↓
DOM mutation
  ↓
DOM mutation
  ↓
...
  ↓
callback ends
  ↓
browser gets a later opportunity to render

This is why code that repeatedly mutates the DOM inside one long task can produce a very different visual result from code that yields control between chunks of work.

17. requestAnimationFrame belongs to the rendering side of the story

requestAnimationFrame() gives you a callback intended to run before a browser repaint opportunity.

requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  // update visual state
});

This does not mean:

“run this function exactly every 16.67 ms.”

It is better understood as:

“schedule this callback for a suitable opportunity before the browser's next rendering update.”

The browser may adapt the timing based on the display, page visibility, workload, throttling, and other factors.

This is a different scheduling intention from:

setTimeout(fn, 16);

which is a timer request, not a rendering synchronization primitive.

18. A complete simplified event-loop picture

             BROWSER RUNTIME
                    │
       ┌────────────┼────────────┐
       │            │            │
    user input    timers      network /
       │            │         other host work
       └────────────┼────────────┘
                    ↓
             runnable task work
                    │
                    ▼
             main JavaScript
                 executes
                    │
                    ▼
          microtask checkpoint
                    │
                    ▼
        browser scheduling / possible
          rendering opportunity
                    │
                    ▼
             next scheduled work

This is a simplified mental model, not a literal standards algorithm. The important hierarchy is:

host produces work
        ↓
scheduler determines when JS gets a turn
        ↓
JavaScript runs synchronously
        ↓
microtasks are processed at their checkpoints
        ↓
browser can perform other work / rendering
        ↓
another turn occurs

19. Use this model to predict real code instead of memorizing rules

Consider:

console.log("1");

setTimeout(() => console.log("2"), 0);

queueMicrotask(() => console.log("3"));

Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("4"));

console.log("5");

First ask: what runs in the current synchronous task?

1
5

Then ask: what microtasks are waiting?

3
4

Then ask: what ordinary task remains?

2

So the expected conceptual ordering is:

1
5
3
4
2

The important skill is not memorizing this one answer. It is decomposing the program into:

current task
→ microtasks
→ later task

20. What you can explain after Node 4 — and what Node 4 intentionally leaves broken

You should now be able to explain:

event loop
    = host scheduling model coordinating runnable work

task
    = one category of scheduled work

microtask
    = work processed at microtask checkpoints

setTimeout(fn, 0)
    = schedule timer work; not immediate execution

Promise.then(...)
    = promise reaction scheduled as microtask work

requestAnimationFrame(...)
    = rendering-oriented callback scheduling

main thread
    = where ordinary page JavaScript gets its execution turn

You should also be able to explain why:

setTimeout(..., 0)
```

does not beat:


Promise.resolve().then(...)



just because the timer was registered first.



The deeper mental model is:



JavaScript does not independently decide when it runs. The browser host determines when the JavaScript execution context gets a turn. Different sources of work enter different scheduling mechanisms, and microtask checkpoints create ordering guarantees inside that larger scheduling system.



But now another layer becomes unavoidable.



We know what the scheduler does at a high level, but we still have not explained the different sources of work in enough detail.



What exactly happens to a network operation after fetch() is called?



Where does the network work actually happen?



What does it mean for a response to “complete” if JavaScript is currently busy?



Why can a fetch continue while the main JavaScript thread is blocked?



What exactly gets queued when the network completes?



How do promises connect the network completion to a microtask?



What's still broken: we now have the scheduling framework, but we have not yet traced an asynchronous operation from the JavaScript call through host machinery and back into the JavaScript event loop. The next node will use networking/fetch as the concrete case that connects host-side asynchronous work to JavaScript scheduling.

'
